{{Short description|Belgian mathematician (1561–1615)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2019}}
'''Adriaan van Roomen''' (29 September 1561 – 4 May 1615), also known as '''Adrianus Romanus''', was a mathematician, professor of medicine and [[medical astrology|medical astrologer]] from the [[Duchy of Brabant]] in the [[Habsburg Netherlands]] who was active throughout Central Europe in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. As a mathematician he worked in algebra, trigonometry and geometry; and on the [[decimal expansion]] of [[pi]]. He solved the [[Problem of Apollonius]] using a new method that involved intersecting hyperbolas. He also wrote on the [[Gregorian calendar reform]].

==Life==
Van Roomen was born in [[Leuven]], the son of Adriaan Van Roomen and Maria Van Den Daele. He was educated partly in Leuven and partly After studying at the Jesuit College in [[Cologne]], also attending the [[University of Cologne]] where he began his study of medicine.<ref name=Bosmans>Henri Bosmans, "Romain (Adrien)", ''[[Biographie Nationale de Belgique]]'', [https://www.academieroyale.be/Academie/documents/FichierPDFBiographieNationaleTome2064.pdf vol. 19] (Brussels), 848-888.</ref> He also briefly studied medicine at [[Old University of Leuven|Leuven University]]. Roomen was professor of mathematics and medicine at Louvain from 1586 to 1592. He met [[Kepler]], and discussed with [[François Viète]] two questions about equations and tangencies. He then spent some time in Italy, particularly with [[Clavius]] in [[Rome]] in 1585. His publication of 1595, ''Parvum theatrum urbium'', contained Latin verse on the cities of Italy (possibly written by [[Thomas Edwards (poet)|Thomas Edwards]]).<ref name=ODNB>Matthew Steggle, 'Edwards, Thomas ([[floruit|fl.]] 1587–1595)’, [[Oxford Dictionary of National Biography]], Oxford University Press, 2004</ref>

In June 1593 Van Roomen became the inaugural professor of medicine at the newly refounded [[University of Würzburg]].<ref name=Bosmans/> He was also appointed physician in ordinary to the court of [[Rudolf II]].<ref name=Bosmans/> From around 1595 to 1603 he produced calendars, almanacs and prognostications published under the patronage of [[Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn|Julius Echter]], [[prince-bishop of Würzburg]].<ref>Paul Bockstaele, "Astrologie te Leuven in de zeventiende eeuw", ''De Zeventiende Eeuw'', 5 (1989), [https://www.dbnl.org/tekst/_zev001198901_01/_zev001198901_01_0018.php pp. 172-180].</ref> At the same time, he served as mathematician of the king of Poland and become famous for the computation of the value of [[pi]] to sixteen decimals,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Roomen/|title=Adriaan van Roomen|website=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive|MacTutor]]}}</ref><ref name="PMC7927718">{{cite journal|first1=David Eugene|last1=Smith|author-link1=David Eugene Smith|title=Medicine and Mathematics in the Sixteenth Century|pmc=7927718|pmid= 33943138|journal=Ann. Med. Hist.|date=July 1, 1917|volume= 1|issue=2|pages=125–140|oclc=12650954}} (here cited p. 131).</ref> surpassing [[François Viète]] who had arrived at ten digits.<ref>{{cite web|first1=Maarten|last1=Bullynck|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01717707/document|title=The 'Everyday' in Mathematics On the usability of mathematical practices for doing history|page=10|year=2018|website=[[Hal.archives-ouvertes.fr]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200709053623/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01717707/document|archive-date=9 July 2020|url-status=live|access-date=16 July 2021}}</ref> After being widowed he was ordained to the priesthood in 1604 and on 8 October 1608 was installed as a canon of the [[collegiate church]] of St John the Evangelist in Würzburg.<ref name=Bosmans/>

His ''Mathesis Polemica'', published in Frankfurt in 1605, explained the military applications of mathematics. In June 1610 he was in Prague, after which he travelled to Poland at the invitation of [[Jan Zamoyski]] to give public lectures on mathematics at [[Zamość]] in [[Red Ruthenia]]. He made the return journey via Hungary, arriving back in Würzburg at the end of 1611.<ref name=Bosmans/>

Struggling with health problems, Van Roomen undertook a journey to [[Spa, Belgium|Spa]] to take the waters but died en route at [[Mainz]] in the arms of his son, who was travelling with him.<ref name=Bosmans/>
